result: The Ras-GTPase regulator gefE is required for normal lineage priming and salt and pepper differentiation by setting the intrinsic response threshold to DIF-dependent differentiation signals. GefE regulates context-dependent/relative DIF-dependent lineage bias rather than cell fate commitment.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C20, C26, and C30 collectively establish that gefE is required for lineage priming (not commitment) and that it functions by setting DIF response thresholds. The evidence from chimeric development (Figures 1-3) and clonal development (Figure 3A-B) strongly supports the distinction between priming and commitment, as gefE− mutants show normal clonal development but altered lineage bias in chimeras.

result: Cells grown without glucose (G−) are biased towards DIF-dependent pstO and pstB lineages and produce fewer spores in chimeric development. The gefE− mutant suppresses this glucose-dependent lineage bias.
evaluation: Claims C8-C10 establish the glucose-dependent lineage bias with quantitative data (Figure 1A-B, p<0.0001). Claims C15-C16 demonstrate that gefE− mutation suppresses this bias (Figure 1E-F, p<0.04). The statistical significance and imaging data provide strong support for these observations.

result: A genetic screen using REMI mutagenesis identified gefE as a regulator of lineage bias. The gefE− mutant shows no growth rate differences but exhibits faster spore hatching compared to wild type.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12 describe the genetic screen methodology and identification of gefE (Figure 1C-D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B). Claims C13-C14 characterize the mutant phenotype with quantitative data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C-D). The approach is sound and the characterization is thorough.

result: gefE− mutant cells avoid DIF-dependent prestalk fates (pstO and pstB) and are enriched in prespore regions when grown under identical conditions and mixed with wild type cells. Overexpression of GefE drives cells toward DIF-dependent fates.
evaluation: Claims C17-C19 demonstrate the cell fate bias of gefE− mutants with quantitative spore counts (Figure 2A, p<0.01) and imaging data (Figure 2B-C, Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2). The reciprocal experiment with GefE overexpression (C19) provides strong support for the conclusion in C20.

result: gefE− mutant cells are totipotent and show normal clonal development with proper cell type proportions and gene expression. The only defect is a slight delay in aggregation initiation. This demonstrates that gefE regulates lineage priming rather than commitment.
evaluation: Claims C21-C25 establish normal clonal development with quantitative data (Figure 3A-B). Claims C26, C29, and C30 draw the appropriate conclusion that gefE affects priming not commitment. The logic is sound: if gefE were required for commitment, clonal development would be defective, but it is not.

result: The lineage bias of gefE− mutant cells is context-dependent and determined by the growth history of the partner genotype in chimeric development.
evaluation: Claims C27-C28 demonstrate that gefE− mutants can be biased toward DIF-dependent fates when mixed with gefE− cells grown in different conditions (Figure 3C). This provides strong evidence for the context-dependent nature of the bias and supports the priming model.

result: gefE− mutant cells are less sensitive to DIF than wild type cells across a 1000-fold concentration range, but exhibit similar sensitivity to changes in DIF concentration. GefE sets basal levels of DIF sensitivity and biases cells toward DIF-sensitive fates.
evaluation: Claims C31-C34 establish the DIF sensitivity phenotype with dose-response data (Figure 4A). The parallel dose-response curves support the interpretation that GefE sets basal sensitivity without affecting the response to concentration changes. Claims C41-C42 appropriately summarize the findings.

result: DIF-induced expression of prestalk genes (ecmA, ecmB) and nuclear translocation of the transcription factor GATAc are reduced in gefE− mutants. Fewer gefE− cells respond to DIF, but the rate and duration of GATAc translocation in responding cells are unaffected.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 demonstrate reduced DIF-induced gene expression with reporter assays and qPCR (Figure 4B-C). Claims C37-C40 show that fewer gefE− cells exhibit GATAc nuclear translocation, but the kinetics in responding cells are normal (Figure 4D). This supports a threshold model rather than a signaling defect.

result: gefE regulates the cell-intrinsic threshold at which cells respond to DIF. Using an ecmA:GFP knock-in and FACS analysis, the authors show that gefE− mutants have fewer responding cells at all DIF concentrations, but responding cells express similar levels of ecmA:GFP as wild type.
evaluation: Claims C43-C44 establish the hypothesis based on prior work. Claims C45-C48 present the experimental test using a novel ecmA:GFP knock-in approach (Figure 5A-D). The FACS data clearly show fewer responding gefE− cells with similar per-cell expression levels, strongly supporting the threshold model in C49. This is a key mechanistic result.

result: GefE is the predominant and specific activator of RasD. RasD is the only Ras protein with strong developmental expression, and both RasD expression and RasD-GTP levels are higher in G− cells. In gefE− mutants, RasD-GTP levels are significantly reduced without affecting total RasD or other Ras proteins.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 establish the rationale for focusing on RasD. Claims C55-C58 demonstrate the biochemical relationship between GefE and RasD with Western blot data (Figure 6A-B). The specificity for RasD (C57) and the lack of effect on total RasD levels (C56) strongly support the conclusion that GefE specifically activates RasD.

result: RasD mutants phenocopy gefE mutants in chimeric development. Overexpression or constitutive activation of RasD drives cells toward DIF-dependent fates in a GefE-dependent manner. GefE and RasD coordinate DIF-dependent lineage bias.
evaluation: Claims C59-C61 demonstrate the genetic relationship between GefE and RasD with chimeric development experiments (Figure 6C-D). The requirement for constitutively active RasD(G12T) to bypass gefE− (C61) strongly supports the model that GefE activates RasD. Claims C62-C63 appropriately conclude that GefE and RasD function together.

result: gefE expression is uniform during growth, while rasD expression is highly heterogeneous. Growth in G− medium increases the proportion of rasD-expressing cells without affecting gefE expression. The rasD promoter reporter shows appropriate developmental regulation.
evaluation: Claims C5, C64-C65 establish the differential expression patterns with reporter gene imaging (Figure 7A). Claim C66 validates the rasD reporter. Claims C67-C68 show that glucose affects rasD but not gefE expression. The imaging data clearly support these observations, providing a mechanism for heterogeneous lineage priming.

result: Cells expressing low levels of rasD are less likely to become prestalk cells. FACS-sorted rasD high and low populations return to equilibrium when regrown, indicating dynamic rasD expression. Nutritional history affects the position of this dynamic equilibrium.
evaluation: Claims C69-C72 present FACS sorting and fate-tracking experiments (Figure 7B-C). However, C70 notes that high rasD cells can form both cell types, which the authors attribute to potential differences in RasD and RFP protein stability. This caveat undermines the strength of the fate-tracking experiment. While C71-C72 show return to equilibrium (supporting dynamic expression), the interpretation of C69-C70 regarding fate bias is uncertain due to the reporter limitations acknowledged by the authors.

result: Heterogeneous rasD transcription in growing cells, combined with ubiquitous GefE expression, generates a subset of cells with activated RasD. This RasD activation sets the threshold for DIF response and determines lineage bias.
evaluation: Claims C75-C78 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model. The evidence from reporter gene expression (C75, Figure 7A), uniform gefE expression (C76, Figure 7A), reduced RasD-GTP in gefE− mutants (C77, Figure 6B), and DIF threshold experiments (C78, Figures 4-5) collectively support this model. This represents the key mechanistic insight of the paper.

result: Previous studies on Ras signaling in Dictyostelium development were inconclusive. The current work resolves this by showing that GefE-mediated activation of RasD is uniquely important for lineage bias, and that compensatory upregulation of RasG does not affect lineage bias in chimeras.
evaluation: Claims C79-C80 accurately cite prior work. Claims C81-C82 address the compensation issue with data (stated but not shown). Claim C83 draws an appropriate conclusion. However, the lack of shown data for C81-C82 is a weakness. The conclusion is reasonable but would be stronger with the supporting data.

result: Heterogeneous cell behavior and lineage priming in cell culture may reflect mechanisms used during normal embryonic development. Salt and pepper differentiation followed by sorting out is proposed as a fundamental developmental patterning mechanism conserved from Dictyostelium to mammals.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C84-C87 establish the broader context by citing relevant literature on heterogeneous cell behavior in culture and mouse development. The comparison between Dictyostelium and mouse ICM development (C84-C85) is well-supported by citations. Claim C86 appropriately frames the significance of studying this mechanism in Dictyostelium.

result: Dictyostelium development involves salt and pepper differentiation of prestalk and prespore cells followed by sorting. DIF is required for pstB and pstO cell differentiation, and cells show heterogeneous sensitivity to DIF with all-or-none responses.
evaluation: Claims C88-C94 provide essential background on Dictyostelium development and DIF signaling, supported by appropriate citations. This background is accurate and necessary for understanding the experimental system. These are established facts in the field.

result: Cells grown without glucose preferentially become stalk cells and are more sensitive to DIF than glucose-grown cells, as established by previous studies.
evaluation: Claims C7 and C10 cite prior work and are confirmed by the current study's data (Figure 1, Figure 4A). This establishes the experimental foundation for the genetic screen. The citations are appropriate and the phenomenon is well-established.

result: Dictyostelium strains were cultured in defined conditions with or without glucose, and transformants were selected with appropriate antibiotics.
evaluation: Claims C95-C97 describe standard methods that are clearly stated and appropriate for the experiments. These are routine procedures in Dictyostelium research and are adequately described.
